name: Coffee
title: From forest to coffeehouse
intro: Follow arabica from its East African roots through the Red Sea to the coffeehouses of London.
stops: Arabica coffee grew wild in Ethiopia. Its journey begins in the highlands, where the plant was already part of local life before it became a commodity traded across oceans.
A port gives coffee its name
Yemen became an early centre of coffee cultivation and trade. Merchants bought beans through Mocha, a Red Sea port whose name became associated with the drink.
Coffeehouses appeared in London in the mid-seventeenth century. A drink carried across trading networks gave customers a new place to meet, talk and exchange news.

name: Black pepper
title: The spice that crossed oceans
intro: Trace one branch of the pepper trade from India’s Malabar Coast around southern Africa to Lisbon.
stops: A market on the Malabar Coast
Kozhikode, historically called Calicut, was already a busy Indian Ocean port when Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498. Pepper grown in the region passed through established merchant networks.
Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
The Portuguese route linked the Atlantic and Indian Oceans by rounding southern Africa. Ships could carry pepper toward Europe without relying on the same chain of ports used in Mediterranean trade.
Portuguese merchants brought Malabar pepper to Lisbon. The route shifted part of the European trade toward Atlantic ports while other routes continued to operate.

name: The potato
title: A highland crop crosses the Atlantic
intro: Follow a crop that Andean farmers diversified long before it reached Europe.
stops: A crop adapted to the highlands
Andean communities cultivated many kinds of potatoes. Different varieties and ways of preserving them helped make the crop a dependable food in the highlands.
Early records place potatoes in the Canary Islands in the sixteenth century. The islands offer a clue to how the crop travelled on shipping routes linking the Americas and Europe.
From a new arrival to a staple
Early records in mainland Spain include purchases for a hospital in Seville. Farmers and gardeners helped the crop spread over time, long before it became an everyday food across much of Europe.

name: Paper
title: How a craft travelled west
intro: Trace the spread of papermaking across workshops, trading cities and writing cultures.
stops: Papermakers in China learned to turn plant fibres into thin sheets. The craft could travel wherever people had suitable fibres, water and the knowledge to work them.
Samarkand became known for papermaking. A familiar story ties the craft’s spread to a single battle, but the route here shows centres of production without assigning the transfer to one event.
Papermaking reached Baghdad during the Abbasid era. Paper supported the work of scribes and book producers as the craft spread to other cities.
European papermakers developed their own workshop methods. Italian centres such as Fabriano became known for paper production and for using watermarks to identify sheets.

name: Transatlantic cable
title: When a message outran a ship
intro: Follow the 1866 telegraph cable from the Irish coast to Newfoundland, with a stop in the open Atlantic.
stops: A cable briefly worked in 1858 before failing. Engineers tried again, and in July 1866 the Great Eastern began paying out a new cable from Valentia.
A cable could break under its own weight as it sank. Crews had to control the rate at which it ran off the ship. An attempt in 1865 had already ended with a break at sea.
The cable reached Heart’s Content on July 27, 1866. Once connected to telegraph networks on both shores, news could cross the ocean in minutes instead of waiting for the next ship.
